```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source(here::here("blog", "_R", "post_setup.R"))

install_missing_packages(c(
  "tidyverse", "uwot", "highcharter", "htmltools", "dbscan",
  "rpart", "rpart.plot", "knitr", "scales"
))
```

A long time ago, when I was younger, I knew the original 150 Pokémon.
Then the Pokédex kept growing: new generations, new types, new regions and a
lot more monsters to remember.

In 2016 I downloaded the data and used it as an excuse to make charts and try
a dimensionality-reduction method I had just discovered. The code got old, the
links disappeared, but the question remained fun: **what does the Pokémon
universe look like when similarity becomes a map?**

::: {.column-body}
![I have no idea](images/ihavenoidea.gif){width=72% fig-align="center"}
:::

This version keeps the spirit of the
[original post](https://github.com/jbkunst/jbkunst.github.io2/blob/master/_posts/2016-03-08-pokemon-visualize-em-all.md),
but uses the data pipeline behind the
[Pokémon Dimensionality Reduction app](https://jbkunst-pokemon-dimensionality-reduction.share.connect.posit.cloud/),
all nine generations, UMAP, and one extra question: once the map exists, **can
we explain why it looks that way?**

## Data

The data preparation used here is copied from the application. It downloads the
maintained PokeAPI tables, joins battle stats, morphology, capture and breeding
traits, egg groups, species metadata, types and generation, adds the sprite
URLs, builds the mixed feature matrix, and caches the result as an RDS file.

The post reads the cached file so rendering does not depend on a collection of
remote downloads. To rebuild it, the complete procedure lives next to this
article in [`prepare_data.R`](prepare_data.R).

```{r rebuild-pokemon-data}
#| eval: false
# Rebuild only when the PokeAPI source data needs to be refreshed.
source("prepare_data.R")
prepare_pokemon_data(
  cache_file = "data/pokemon-data.rds",
  refresh = TRUE
)
```

```{r load-pokemon-data}
library(tidyverse)
library(highcharter)

source("prepare_data.R", local = TRUE)

pokemon_bundle <- readRDS("data/pokemon-data.rds")

pokemon <- pokemon_bundle$data |>
  filter(generation_id %in% 1:9) |>
  mutate(
    generation_label = factor(
      paste("Generation", generation_id),
      levels = paste("Generation", 1:9)
    ),
    pokemon_label = pokemon |>
      str_replace_all("-", " ") |>
      str_to_title(),
    type_2 = replace_na(type_2, "none")
  )

type_palette <- pokemon |>
  distinct(type_1, type_color) |>
  deframe()

pokemon |>
  select(
    id, pokemon_label, generation_label, type_1, type_2,
    hp, attack, defense, special_attack, special_defense, speed
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 6)
```

There are `r scales::comma(nrow(pokemon))` Pokémon in the analysis.

### A quick generation refresher

I still know Generation I by heart. After that I need reminders. The starter
list below is a small explicit lookup; legendary and mythical Pokémon come
straight from the species flags in the prepared PokeAPI data. The table means
*introduced in that generation*, not every Pokémon obtainable in every game.

```{r pokemon-generation-guide}
starters <- tribble(
  ~generation_id, ~starters,
  1, "Bulbasaur · Charmander · Squirtle",
  2, "Chikorita · Cyndaquil · Totodile",
  3, "Treecko · Torchic · Mudkip",
  4, "Turtwig · Chimchar · Piplup",
  5, "Snivy · Tepig · Oshawott",
  6, "Chespin · Fennekin · Froakie",
  7, "Rowlet · Litten · Popplio",
  8, "Grookey · Scorbunny · Sobble",
  9, "Sprigatito · Fuecoco · Quaxly"
)

generation_guide <- pokemon |>
  group_by(generation_id, generation_label) |>
  summarise(
    legendary = str_c(
      pokemon_label[is_legendary %in% TRUE],
      collapse = " · "
    ),
    mythical = str_c(
      pokemon_label[is_mythical %in% TRUE],
      collapse = " · "
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(starters, by = "generation_id") |>
  select(generation = generation_label, starters, legendary, mythical)

knitr::kable(generation_guide)
```

### How did the Pokédex grow?

The generations are not equally large. A single blue bar would be a poor
choice here: blue already means Water in the Pokémon palette. Stacking the
primary types keeps the total size of each generation while also showing how
its composition changed.

```{r plot-pokemon-counts}
#| column: page
generation_counts <- pokemon |>
  count(generation_label, type_1)

type_counts <- pokemon |>
  count(type_1, type_color, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(type_1 = fct_reorder(type_1, n))

plot_generation_counts <- ggplot(
  generation_counts,
  aes(generation_label, n, fill = type_1)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = type_palette) +
  labs(
    title = "The Pokédex did not grow at the same pace",
    subtitle = "Each bar is stacked by primary type",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Pokémon",
    fill = "Primary type"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  ) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE))

plot_type_counts <- ggplot(
  type_counts,
  aes(n, type_1, fill = type_color)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  labs(
    title = "Water is still a crowded neighborhood",
    x = "Pokémon",
    y = NULL
  )

plot_generation_counts
plot_type_counts
```

Primary type is only half of the story. Flying, for example, can look uncommon
when we count only the first slot even though it appears often as a secondary
type. The matrix below keeps **every Pokémon**, including monotypes. `Only`
means there is no second type.

```{r pokemon-type-combinations}
#| column: page
mix_type_colors <- function(color_1, color_2) {
  purrr::map2_chr(color_1, color_2, function(a, b) {
    if (is.na(b)) return(a)

    rgb <- (grDevices::col2rgb(a) + grDevices::col2rgb(b)) / 2
    grDevices::rgb(rgb[1], rgb[2], rgb[3], maxColorValue = 255)
  })
}

secondary_palette <- pokemon |>
  distinct(type_1, type_color) |>
  rename(type_2 = type_1, type_2_color = type_color)

type_combinations <- pokemon |>
  count(type_1, type_2, name = "n") |>
  mutate(secondary_type = if_else(type_2 == "none", "Only", type_2)) |>
  left_join(
    pokemon |>
      distinct(type_1, type_color),
    by = "type_1"
  ) |>
  left_join(secondary_palette, by = "type_2") |>
  mutate(
    combination_color = mix_type_colors(type_color, type_2_color),
    combination = if_else(
      secondary_type == "Only",
      str_to_title(type_1),
      paste(str_to_title(type_1), "+", str_to_title(secondary_type))
    )
  )

primary_levels <- sort(unique(type_combinations$type_1))
secondary_levels <- c(
  "Only",
  sort(setdiff(unique(type_combinations$secondary_type), "Only"))
)

heatmap_data <- type_combinations |>
  transmute(
    x = match(type_1, primary_levels) - 1L,
    y = match(secondary_type, secondary_levels) - 1L,
    value = n,
    name = combination,
    color = combination_color
  ) |>
  purrr::pmap(as.list) |>
  unname()

highchart() |>
  hc_chart(type = "heatmap", backgroundColor = "transparent") |>
  hc_title(text = "Primary and secondary types") |>
  hc_subtitle(text = "Cell color blends both type colors · Only = monotype") |>
  hc_xAxis(
    categories = str_to_title(primary_levels),
    title = list(text = "Primary type")
  ) |>
  hc_yAxis(
    categories = str_to_title(secondary_levels),
    title = list(text = "Secondary type")
  ) |>
  hc_add_series(
    data = heatmap_data,
    type = "heatmap",
    name = "Pokémon",
    borderWidth = 1,
    borderColor = "#FFFFFF",
    dataLabels = list(
      enabled = TRUE,
      format = "{point.value}",
      style = list(textOutline = "none", fontWeight = 500)
    )
  ) |>
  hc_tooltip(
    headerFormat = "",
    pointFormat = "<b>{point.name}</b><br>{point.value} Pokémon"
  ) |>
  hc_colorAxis(visible = FALSE) |>
  hc_legend(enabled = FALSE) |>
  hc_credits(enabled = FALSE) |>
  hc_size(height = 760)
```

## What makes two Pokémon similar?

The app uses a mixed feature space. Continuous variables are median-imputed and
standardized; binary variables remain 0/1; egg groups and species traits are
one-hot encoded. Each semantic block is divided by the square root of its
number of columns so a wide dummy block does not dominate Euclidean distance
just because it contains more columns.

For this post I make one deliberate change to the app recipe. These labels are
**not allowed to build the map**:

- `type`;
- `generation`;
- `is_legendary`;
- `is_mythical`.

Type and generation were already excluded. Legendary and mythical are removed
here too because I want to see whether Pokémon given those labels end up near
each other because of their other characteristics, not because the label was
fed into the algorithm.

```{r prepare-umap-features}
#| code-fold: true
pokemon_map_feature_matrix <- function(
  data,
  block_weights = c(
    continuous = 1,
    binary = 1,
    egg_groups = 1,
    species_traits = 1
  )
) {
  feature_data <- data |>
    mutate(
      female_ratio = if_else(
        gender_rate < 0,
        NA_real_,
        as.numeric(gender_rate) / 8
      ),
      genderless = as.numeric(gender_rate < 0)
    )

  continuous_features <- feature_data |>
    select(
      height, weight, base_experience,
      hp, attack, defense, special_attack, special_defense, speed,
      capture_rate, base_happiness, hatch_counter, female_ratio
    ) |>
    scale_continuous_features() |>
    weight_feature_block(block_weights[["continuous"]])

  binary_features <- feature_data |>
    transmute(
      is_baby = as.numeric(replace_na(is_baby, 0)),
      has_gender_differences = as.numeric(
        replace_na(has_gender_differences, 0)
      ),
      forms_switchable = as.numeric(replace_na(forms_switchable, 0)),
      genderless = as.numeric(replace_na(genderless, 0))
    ) |>
    as.matrix() |>
    weight_feature_block(block_weights[["binary"]])

  egg_group_features <- feature_data |>
    transmute(
      egg_group_1 = factor(replace_na(egg_group_1, "none")),
      egg_group_2 = factor(replace_na(egg_group_2, "none"))
    ) |>
    model.matrix(~ egg_group_1 + egg_group_2 - 1, data = _) |>
    weight_feature_block(block_weights[["egg_groups"]])

  species_trait_features <- feature_data |>
    transmute(
      growth_rate = factor(replace_na(growth_rate, "unknown")),
      body_color = factor(replace_na(body_color, "unknown")),
      body_shape = factor(replace_na(body_shape, "unknown")),
      habitat = factor(replace_na(habitat, "unknown"))
    ) |>
    model.matrix(
      ~ growth_rate + body_color + body_shape + habitat - 1,
      data = _
    ) |>
    weight_feature_block(block_weights[["species_traits"]])

  features <- cbind(
    continuous_features,
    binary_features,
    egg_group_features,
    species_trait_features
  )

  storage.mode(features) <- "double"
  features
}

features <- pokemon_map_feature_matrix(pokemon)
dim(features)
```

The important point is that UMAP does not start with distances between the two
coordinates we eventually draw. It first sees the high-dimensional matrix
above. With the Euclidean metric, the raw distance that feeds its neighborhood
construction begins with

$$
d^2(i,j) = \sum_k (x_{ik} - x_{jk})^2.
$$

UMAP then uses local neighborhoods and turns that high-dimensional structure
into the two-dimensional map. The final axes do not have a direct physical
meaning.

## A Wild UMAP Appears!

```{r fit-pokemon-umap}
set.seed(13242)

umap_coordinates <- uwot::umap(
  features,
  n_neighbors = 30,
  min_dist = 0.15,
  metric = "euclidean",
  n_components = 2,
  n_threads = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)

pokemon <- pokemon |>
  mutate(
    umap_1 = umap_coordinates[, 1],
    umap_2 = umap_coordinates[, 2]
  )
```

First, the complete map. Type is only a color: it did not participate in the
UMAP calculation. Neither did generation, legendary or mythical status.

```{r plot-overall-umap}
#| column: page
ggplot(pokemon, aes(umap_1, umap_2, color = type_1)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.9, alpha = 0.72) +
  scale_color_manual(values = type_palette) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "A Wild UMAP Appears!",
    subtitle = "Type, generation, legendary and mythical status are excluded",
    color = "Primary type",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

The colors are not perfectly separated—and they should not be. Still, some
types occupy more compact neighborhoods while others spread across the map.
That is evidence of association between type and the traits used here, not a
claim that type is determined by them.

## Who's That Neighbor?

A two-dimensional UMAP can make two sprites look close, but the more useful
question is: **what made them neighbors before the projection?** I use the same
weighted feature matrix and Euclidean metric that UMAP receives, find nearest
neighbors there, and then decompose the squared distance into its original
pieces.

```{r find-pokemon-neighbors}
feature_distances <- as.matrix(stats::dist(features, method = "euclidean"))
diag(feature_distances) <- Inf

nearest_neighbor <- function(pokemon_name, example) {
  i <- match(pokemon_name, pokemon$pokemon)
  stopifnot(!is.na(i))
  j <- which.min(feature_distances[i, ])

  tibble(
    example,
    anchor = pokemon$pokemon[i],
    neighbor = pokemon$pokemon[j],
    distance = feature_distances[i, j]
  )
}

neighbor_pairs <- bind_rows(
  nearest_neighbor("bulbasaur", "Bulbasaur's nearest neighbor"),
  nearest_neighbor("snorlax", "Snorlax's nearest neighbor")
)

cross_type_distances <- feature_distances
same_primary_type <- outer(pokemon$type_1, pokemon$type_1, FUN = "==")
cross_type_distances[same_primary_type] <- Inf
cross_type_distances[lower.tri(cross_type_distances, diag = TRUE)] <- Inf

cross_type_position <- arrayInd(
  which.min(cross_type_distances),
  dim(cross_type_distances)
)

neighbor_pairs <- bind_rows(
  neighbor_pairs,
  tibble(
    example = "Closest pair with different primary types",
    anchor = pokemon$pokemon[cross_type_position[1]],
    neighbor = pokemon$pokemon[cross_type_position[2]],
    distance = cross_type_distances[cross_type_position[1], cross_type_position[2]]
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    anchor = str_to_title(str_replace_all(anchor, "-", " ")),
    neighbor = str_to_title(str_replace_all(neighbor, "-", " "))
  )

knitr::kable(neighbor_pairs, digits = 3)
```

The number alone says *how far apart* two profiles are. To understand *why*, I
group the squared differences back into readable variables. Dummy columns for
egg groups, habitat, body color, body shape and growth rate are recombined into
the concepts they represent.

```{r explain-pokemon-neighbors}
feature_group <- function(feature) {
  case_when(
    str_starts(feature, "egg_group_") ~ "Egg groups",
    str_starts(feature, "growth_rate") ~ "Growth rate",
    str_starts(feature, "body_color") ~ "Body color",
    str_starts(feature, "body_shape") ~ "Body shape",
    str_starts(feature, "habitat") ~ "Habitat",
    TRUE ~ feature |>
      str_replace_all("_", " ") |>
      str_to_title()
  )
}

explain_pair <- function(example, anchor, neighbor, distance) {
  anchor_key <- anchor |> str_to_lower() |> str_replace_all(" ", "-")
  neighbor_key <- neighbor |> str_to_lower() |> str_replace_all(" ", "-")
  i <- match(anchor_key, pokemon$pokemon)
  j <- match(neighbor_key, pokemon$pokemon)

  tibble(
    feature = colnames(features),
    squared_difference = (features[i, ] - features[j, ])^2
  ) |>
    mutate(feature = feature_group(feature)) |>
    summarise(
      squared_difference = sum(squared_difference),
      .by = feature
    ) |>
    mutate(
      contribution = squared_difference / sum(squared_difference),
      example = paste(anchor, "↔", neighbor)
    )
}

neighbor_contributions <- purrr::pmap_dfr(
  neighbor_pairs,
  explain_pair
)

neighbor_contributions |>
  group_by(example) |>
  slice_max(contribution, n = 6, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(contribution, fct_reorder(feature, contribution))) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(vars(example), scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "What separates each pair?",
    subtitle = "Largest contributions to squared Euclidean distance",
    x = "Share of distance",
    y = NULL
  )
```

A short bar means that characteristic contributes little to separating the
pair; a long bar points to the variables where they differ. This is not an
explanation of a UMAP axis. It is an explanation of the original distance that
helped define the neighborhood UMAP started from.

## Looking through type

A faceted view makes every primary type visible without losing the global
geometry. All Pokémon remain in the background; the selected type is
highlighted in its own panel.

```{r plot-umap-by-type}
#| column: page
#| fig-format: png
#| fig-asp: 0.8
# Dense repeated point fields are rasterized to keep the page lightweight.
type_levels <- sort(unique(pokemon$type_1))

type_background <- tidyr::crossing(
  control_type = type_levels,
  pokemon |>
    select(umap_1, umap_2)
)

type_foreground <- pokemon |>
  mutate(control_type = type_1)

ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = type_background,
    aes(umap_1, umap_2),
    color = "#D9E0EA",
    size = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.32
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = type_foreground,
    aes(umap_1, umap_2, color = type_1),
    size = 1.15,
    alpha = 0.82,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = type_palette) +
  facet_wrap(vars(control_type), ncol = 5) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "Do types emerge from the remaining traits?",
    subtitle = "Each panel highlights one primary type in the same UMAP",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(0.45, "lines")
  )
```

## Looking through generation

Generation is another control. Because every panel uses the same coordinates,
we can see whether a generation fills the existing space or introduces Pokémon
in more particular regions.

```{r plot-umap-by-generation}
#| column: page
#| fig-format: png
#| fig-asp: 1
# Dense repeated point fields are rasterized to keep the page lightweight.
generation_levels <- levels(pokemon$generation_label)

generation_background <- tidyr::crossing(
  control_generation = generation_levels,
  pokemon |>
    select(umap_1, umap_2)
)

generation_foreground <- pokemon |>
  mutate(control_generation = generation_label)

ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = generation_background,
    aes(umap_1, umap_2),
    color = "#D9E0EA",
    size = 0.42,
    alpha = 0.30
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = generation_foreground,
    aes(umap_1, umap_2, color = type_1),
    size = 1.25,
    alpha = 0.85,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = type_palette) +
  facet_wrap(vars(control_generation), ncol = 3) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "Nine generations in the same space",
    subtitle = "Color still represents primary type",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(0.55, "lines")
  )
```

The panels help distinguish two ideas that are easy to mix up: a generation
can add many Pokémon without creating a completely new region, while a smaller
generation can still contribute unusual profiles.

## A Wild Cluster Appears!

The map looks as if it contains regions, but I do not want to decide in advance
that there must be exactly four of them. HDBSCAN is useful here because it can
find dense regions in the **visible UMAP space** without receiving a fixed
number of clusters, and it can leave ambiguous points as noise.

This is intentionally a clustering of the two-dimensional map. The question is
not "what is the one true clustering of Pokémon?" It is "can I formalize the
regions I am already looking at?"

```{r cluster-umap-space}
#| column: page
umap_clusters <- dbscan::hdbscan(
  as.matrix(pokemon |> select(umap_1, umap_2)),
  minPts = 20
)

pokemon <- pokemon |>
  mutate(
    cluster = umap_clusters$cluster,
    cluster_label = if_else(
      cluster == 0,
      "Noise",
      paste("Cluster", cluster)
    )
  )

cluster_count <- n_distinct(pokemon$cluster[pokemon$cluster > 0])
cluster_levels <- sort(unique(pokemon$cluster_label[pokemon$cluster > 0]))
cluster_palette <- c(
  stats::setNames(scales::hue_pal()(length(cluster_levels)), cluster_levels),
  Noise = "#B8BDC7"
)

ggplot(pokemon, aes(umap_1, umap_2, color = cluster_label)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.9, alpha = 0.78) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cluster_palette) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = paste("HDBSCAN finds", cluster_count, "dense regions"),
    subtitle = "Clustering is performed on the visible two-dimensional UMAP",
    color = NULL,
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

### What is inside each region?

Before naming anything, describe it. Legendary and mythical status are useful
here precisely because they did **not** participate in the UMAP. Type and
generation are also interpretation variables rather than inputs to the map.

```{r summarize-umap-clusters}
top_value <- function(x) {
  names(sort(table(x), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
}

cluster_centers <- pokemon |>
  filter(cluster > 0) |>
  summarise(
    center_x = mean(umap_1),
    center_y = mean(umap_2),
    .by = cluster_label
  )

cluster_representatives <- pokemon |>
  filter(cluster > 0) |>
  left_join(cluster_centers, by = "cluster_label") |>
  mutate(
    center_distance = (umap_1 - center_x)^2 + (umap_2 - center_y)^2
  ) |>
  group_by(cluster_label) |>
  slice_min(center_distance, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(cluster_label, representative = pokemon_label)

cluster_summary <- pokemon |>
  filter(cluster > 0) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    legendary = scales::percent(mean(is_legendary %in% TRUE), accuracy = 1),
    mythical = scales::percent(mean(is_mythical %in% TRUE), accuracy = 1),
    top_primary_type = str_to_title(top_value(type_1)),
    top_generation = top_value(as.character(generation_label)),
    .by = cluster_label
  ) |>
  left_join(cluster_representatives, by = "cluster_label") |>
  arrange(cluster_label)

knitr::kable(cluster_summary)
```

A second summary ignores labels and looks only at numeric characteristics. Each
cell shows the cluster median; the background color standardizes that variable
across clusters, so the strongest contrasts are easy to spot without pretending
that kilograms and attack points share the same scale.

```{r plot-cluster-profiles}
#| column: page
profile_variables <- c(
  "height", "weight", "base_experience",
  "hp", "attack", "defense", "special_attack", "special_defense", "speed",
  "capture_rate", "base_happiness", "hatch_counter"
)

cluster_profiles <- pokemon |>
  filter(cluster > 0) |>
  summarise(
    across(all_of(profile_variables), ~ median(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .by = cluster_label
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    -cluster_label,
    names_to = "characteristic",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  group_by(characteristic) |>
  mutate(
    z = if_else(
      sd(value) > 0,
      (value - mean(value)) / sd(value),
      0
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    characteristic = characteristic |>
      str_replace_all("_", " ") |>
      str_to_title()
  )

ggplot(cluster_profiles, aes(characteristic, cluster_label, fill = z)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(value, 1)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2() +
  labs(
    title = "A profile before a nickname",
    subtitle = "Labels are cluster medians; color is standardized within each characteristic",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Relative\nlevel"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Only after looking at these summaries does it make sense to attach human names
such as *powerhouses*, *small/common*, *legendary-like*, or whatever the data
actually supports. The names should be conclusions, not inputs.

## Can a Small Tree Explain the Map?

There is no direct SHAP value for "why UMAP put this Pokémon in this visible
region" because UMAP + HDBSCAN is not a supervised classifier with a target we
started with. Instead I can fit a small **proxy** model: a deliberately simple
model that tries to reproduce the cluster labels discovered above from the
original characteristics.

$$
\underbrace{X \rightarrow \mathrm{UMAP} \rightarrow \mathrm{HDBSCAN} \rightarrow C}_{\text{discovery}}
$$

$$
\underbrace{X \rightarrow \text{small decision tree} \rightarrow \widehat{C}}_{\text{explanation proxy}}
$$

The tree receives neither type, generation, legendary nor mythical status. If
a depth-three tree reproduces the groups well, its splits give a compact answer
to *what characteristics separate these regions?*

```{r fit-cluster-proxy-tree}
proxy_data <- pokemon |>
  filter(cluster > 0) |>
  transmute(
    id,
    cluster = factor(cluster_label),
    height,
    weight,
    base_experience,
    hp,
    attack,
    defense,
    special_attack,
    special_defense,
    speed,
    capture_rate,
    base_happiness,
    hatch_counter,
    female_ratio = if_else(
      gender_rate < 0,
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(gender_rate) / 8
    ),
    is_baby = factor(replace_na(is_baby, FALSE)),
    has_gender_differences = factor(
      replace_na(has_gender_differences, FALSE)
    ),
    forms_switchable = factor(replace_na(forms_switchable, FALSE)),
    genderless = factor(gender_rate < 0),
    egg_group_1 = factor(replace_na(egg_group_1, "none")),
    egg_group_2 = factor(replace_na(egg_group_2, "none")),
    growth_rate = factor(replace_na(growth_rate, "unknown")),
    body_color = factor(replace_na(body_color, "unknown")),
    body_shape = factor(replace_na(body_shape, "unknown")),
    habitat = factor(replace_na(habitat, "unknown"))
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.numeric),
      ~ replace_na(.x, median(.x, na.rm = TRUE))
    )
  )

set.seed(13242)
proxy_train_ids <- proxy_data |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  slice_sample(prop = 0.75) |>
  ungroup() |>
  pull(id)

proxy_train <- proxy_data |>
  filter(id %in% proxy_train_ids)

proxy_test <- proxy_data |>
  filter(!id %in% proxy_train_ids)

proxy_tree <- rpart::rpart(
  cluster ~ . - id,
  data = proxy_train,
  method = "class",
  control = rpart::rpart.control(
    maxdepth = 3,
    minsplit = 25,
    cp = 0.01,
    xval = 0
  )
)

proxy_prediction <- predict(
  proxy_tree,
  newdata = proxy_test,
  type = "class"
)

proxy_fidelity <- mean(proxy_prediction == proxy_test$cluster)
```

```{r plot-cluster-proxy-tree}
#| column: page
rpart.plot::rpart.plot(
  proxy_tree,
  type = 4,
  extra = 104,
  fallen.leaves = TRUE,
  tweak = 0.9
)
```

On the held-out quarter of Pokémon, this small tree reproduces the discovered
region for `r scales::percent(proxy_fidelity, accuracy = 1)` of observations.
That number is **proxy fidelity**, not predictive accuracy for some real-world
Pokémon label. High fidelity means the visible regions can be summarized by a
few simple rules; lower fidelity means the separation is real but harder to
compress into a tiny tree.

## Explore 'em all

Points are useful for analysis. Sprites are better for exploration. The final
chart uses exactly the same UMAP coordinates, so changing the visual mark does
not change the result.

```{r build-pokemon-highchart}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show chart code"
point_data <- pokemon |>
  transmute(
    x = umap_1,
    y = umap_2,
    pokemon = pokemon_label,
    generation = as.character(generation_label),
    type_1 = str_to_title(type_1),
    type_2 = if_else(type_2 == "none", "—", str_to_title(type_2)),
    type_color,
    height_m = round(height / 10, 1),
    weight_kg = round(weight / 10, 1),
    hp,
    attack,
    defense,
    special_attack,
    special_defense,
    speed,
    capture_rate,
    artwork_url,
    sprite_url
  ) |>
  purrr::pmap(function(
    x, y, pokemon, generation, type_1, type_2, type_color,
    height_m, weight_kg, hp, attack, defense,
    special_attack, special_defense, speed, capture_rate,
    artwork_url, sprite_url
  ) {
    list(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      name = pokemon,
      pokemon = pokemon,
      generation = generation,
      type_1 = type_1,
      type_2 = type_2,
      type_color = type_color,
      height_m = height_m,
      weight_kg = weight_kg,
      hp = hp,
      attack = attack,
      defense = defense,
      special_attack = special_attack,
      special_defense = special_defense,
      speed = speed,
      capture_rate = capture_rate,
      artwork_url = artwork_url,
      marker = list(
        symbol = sprintf("url(%s)", sprite_url),
        width = 28,
        height = 28
      )
    )
  }) |>
  unname()

halo_data <- pokemon |>
  transmute(
    x = umap_1,
    y = umap_2,
    color = scales::alpha(type_color, 0.18)
  ) |>
  purrr::pmap(function(x, y, color) {
    list(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      color = color,
      marker = list(symbol = "circle", radius = 18)
    )
  }) |>
  unname()

point_data_by_type <- split(point_data, pokemon$type_1)
halo_data_by_type <- split(halo_data, pokemon$type_1)

legend_type_focus <- htmlwidgets::JS(
  "function () {
    var chart = this;

    function setFocus(typeKey) {
      chart.series.forEach(function (series) {
        var custom = series.options.custom || {};
        var sameType = custom.typeKey === typeKey;
        var opacity = custom.isHalo ? (sameType ? 1 : 0) :
          (sameType ? 1 : 0.12);
        var group = series.markerGroup || series.group;

        if (group) {
          group.attr({ opacity: opacity });
          if (sameType) group.toFront();
        }
      });
    }

    function resetFocus() {
      chart.series.forEach(function (series) {
        var custom = series.options.custom || {};
        var group = series.markerGroup || series.group;
        if (group) group.attr({ opacity: custom.isHalo ? 0 : 1 });
      });
    }

    chart.series.forEach(function (series) {
      if (!series.options.showInLegend) return;
      var legendGroup = series.legendItem && series.legendItem.group
        ? series.legendItem.group
        : series.legendGroup;
      var element = legendGroup && legendGroup.element;
      if (!element || element.__pokemonTypeFocusBound) return;

      element.__pokemonTypeFocusBound = true;
      element.addEventListener('mouseenter', function () {
        setFocus(series.options.custom.typeKey);
      });
      element.addEventListener('mouseleave', resetFocus);
    });
  }"
)

raise_tooltip <- htmlwidgets::JS(
  "function () {
    var chart = this.series.chart;
    window.setTimeout(function () {
      if (chart.tooltip && chart.tooltip.label) {
        chart.tooltip.label.toFront();
      }
      if (chart.tooltip && chart.tooltip.container) {
        chart.tooltip.container.style.zIndex = 99999;
      }
    }, 0);
  }"
)

pokemon_series <- sort(names(point_data_by_type)) |>
  purrr::map(function(type_key) {
    type_name <- stringr::str_to_title(type_key)
    type_color <- unname(type_palette[[type_key]])
    sprite_id <- paste0("type-", type_key)

    list(
      list(
        data = halo_data_by_type[[type_key]],
        name = paste(type_name, "halo"),
        linkedTo = sprite_id,
        turboThreshold = 0,
        showInLegend = FALSE,
        enableMouseTracking = FALSE,
        opacity = 0,
        states = list(
          inactive = list(opacity = 0),
          hover = list(opacity = 0)
        ),
        custom = list(typeKey = type_key, isHalo = TRUE),
        zIndex = 1
      ),
      list(
        data = point_data_by_type[[type_key]],
        id = sprite_id,
        name = type_name,
        color = type_color,
        marker = list(symbol = "circle", radius = 5),
        turboThreshold = 0,
        showInLegend = TRUE,
        custom = list(typeKey = type_key, isHalo = FALSE),
        zIndex = 2
      )
    )
  }) |>
  purrr::list_flatten()

tooltip <- paste0(
  '<div style="width:270px;padding:12px;font-family:inherit;background-color:rgb(244,246,248)!important;color:#17324d;border-radius:12px;box-shadow:0 8px 24px rgba(23,50,77,.16);opacity:1!important">',
  '<div style="display:flex;gap:12px;align-items:center">',
  '<img src="{point.artwork_url}" style="width:92px;height:92px;object-fit:contain">',
  '<div><div style="font-size:18px;font-weight:600">{point.pokemon}</div>',
  '<div style="font-size:11px;opacity:.65">{point.generation}</div>',
  '<div style="margin-top:5px">',
  '<span style="background:{point.type_color};color:white;padding:2px 7px;border-radius:10px">{point.type_1}</span>',
  '<span style="margin-left:5px">{point.type_2}</span></div>',
  '<div style="margin-top:8px">{point.height_m} m · {point.weight_kg} kg</div>',
  '</div></div>',
  '<table style="width:100%;margin-top:10px;font-size:12px;background-color:rgb(244,246,248)!important;opacity:1!important">',
  '<tr><td>HP</td><td><b>{point.hp}</b></td><td>Attack</td><td><b>{point.attack}</b></td></tr>',
  '<tr><td>Defense</td><td><b>{point.defense}</b></td><td>Speed</td><td><b>{point.speed}</b></td></tr>',
  '<tr><td>Sp. Atk</td><td><b>{point.special_attack}</b></td><td>Sp. Def</td><td><b>{point.special_defense}</b></td></tr>',
  '<tr><td>Capture</td><td colspan="3"><b>{point.capture_rate}</b></td></tr>',
  '</table></div>'
)

pokemon_chart <- highchart() |>
  hc_chart(
    type = "scatter",
    zoomType = "xy",
    panning = list(enabled = TRUE, type = "xy"),
    panKey = "shift",
    backgroundColor = "transparent",
    animation = FALSE,
    events = list(load = legend_type_focus)
  ) |>
  hc_title(text = "A Wild UMAP Appears!") |>
  hc_subtitle(
    text = "Stats, morphology, breeding and species traits · labels excluded"
  ) |>
  hc_xAxis(visible = FALSE) |>
  hc_yAxis(visible = FALSE) |>
  hc_add_series_list(pokemon_series) |>
  hc_legend(
    enabled = TRUE,
    align = "center",
    verticalAlign = "top",
    layout = "horizontal",
    symbolRadius = 5,
    itemStyle = list(fontWeight = 400)
  ) |>
  hc_tooltip(
    useHTML = TRUE,
    outside = TRUE,
    backgroundColor = "rgb(244, 246, 248)",
    style = list(color = "#17324d", opacity = 1),
    borderWidth = 0,
    borderRadius = 12,
    shadow = TRUE,
    padding = 0,
    headerFormat = "",
    pointFormat = tooltip
  ) |>
  hc_plotOptions(
    series = list(
      animation = FALSE,
      point = list(
        events = list(mouseOver = raise_tooltip)
      ),
      states = list(
        inactive = list(opacity = 1),
        hover = list(halo = list(size = 34, opacity = 0.25))
      )
    )
  ) |>
  hc_credits(enabled = FALSE) |>
  hc_size(height = 900)
```

```{r show-pokemon-highchart}
#| column: screen-inset
pokemon_chart
```

Zooming into the chart brings back the pleasure of the original post: evolution
families, extreme stats, strange combinations, and unexpected neighbors are
more interesting than any single global summary.

## Keep exploring

This post fixes one similarity definition so the analysis can go deeper. The
full application lets you compare PCA, t-SNE and UMAP, change generations, and
explore different definitions of similarity. It is part of
[Visual Data Lab](https://jkunst.com/visual-data-lab/), my collection of small
applications and visualization experiments. You can use the embedded version
below or [open the Pokémon explorer in a new
tab](https://jbkunst-pokemon-dimensionality-reduction.share.connect.posit.cloud/).

::: {.column-screen-inset}

  src="https://jbkunst-pokemon-dimensionality-reduction.share.connect.posit.cloud/"

The original conclusion was basically: *nice algorithm to keep testing with
other data*. I still agree :B. This time, at least, the fun part is not only
making the map—it is asking why two Pokémon became neighbors and what separates
the regions that appeared.
